  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "CC/CE", subtitle = "Population-weighted state-year average", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_ic_gap_fit <- ggplot(annual_gap_summary, aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed_ic_ce, color = "Observed"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = expected_ic_ce, color = "Composition-predicted"), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#EFC000", "Composition-predicted" = "black")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "IC/CE", subtitle = "Population-weighted state-year average", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_cc_gap_fit / p_ic_gap_fit &
  theme(legend.position = "top")
Show code 
p_cc_annual_gap <- ggplot(annual_gap_summary, aes(date, cc_ce_gap)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0073C2", alpha = 0.85, width = 300) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "CC/CE Gap", subtitle = "Observed minus composition-predicted", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_ic_annual_gap <- ggplot(annual_gap_summary, aes(date, ic_ce_gap)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_col(fill = "#EFC000", alpha = 0.9, width = 300) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "IC/CE Gap", subtitle = "Observed minus composition-predicted", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_cc_annual_gap / p_ic_annual_gap

With year fixed effects removed, the composition benchmark must account for the time path of claims intensity, and the within \(R^2\) rises substantially (0.71 for CC/CE, 0.67 for IC/CE). The observed and benchmark-predicted lines track each other closely through the late 1990s and 2000s, with the benchmark capturing both the recessionary spikes (2001, 2008–2009) and the subsequent recoveries. However, a systematic divergence emerges after 2014: observed claims intensity falls below the benchmark-predicted path and the gap widens steadily. By 2024–2025, the CC/CE gap reaches \(-0.005\) to \(-0.006\) (roughly 0.5–0.6 percentage points of covered employment), and the IC/CE gap reaches \(-0.040\) to \(-0.042\). The pandemic year (2020) is an outlier in both directions—a brief positive spike as expanded programs temporarily pushed claims intensity above the level historically associated with the unemployment mix, followed by a sharp negative reversal in 2021 as programs expired. The persistent and widening post-2014 negative residual is the central empirical finding: the composition benchmark does not account for the modern shortfall in UI claims intensity, and the magnitude of the unexplained gap has grown over time. Because the composition of unemployment and claims intensity are jointly shaped by broader labor-market and policy shocks, the benchmark prediction should be interpreted as a composition-conditioned reduced-form benchmark, not a causal counterfactual.

Comparison: National Aggregate vs. State Panel

The state-panel gap above uses CPS-based state-level composition and absorbs cross-state level differences via state fixed effects. To isolate how much the state FE and CPS measurement contribute, I collapse the state panel to a single national annual series (population-weighted means) and estimate the same by-cause OLS without fixed effects. The resulting gap is directly comparable to the national annual gap in Section 7.2, but uses CPS-derived shares rather than FRED aggregates.

Show code 
national_from_panel <- panel_year |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    cc_ce = weighted.mean(continued_claims_per_covered_employment, annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    ic_ce = weighted.mean(initial_claims_per_covered_employment, annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    temp_layoff_share    = weighted.mean(temp_layoff_share,    annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    perm_job_loser_share = weighted.mean(perm_job_loser_share, annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    job_leaver_share     = weighted.mean(job_leaver_share,     annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    reentrant_share      = weighted.mean(reentrant_share,      annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    new_entrant_share    = weighted.mean(new_entrant_share,    annual_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(paste0(year, "-01-01")))

collapsed_rhs <- "temp_layoff_share + perm_job_loser_share + job_leaver_share + reentrant_share + new_entrant_share"

cc_collapsed <- lm(as.formula(paste0("cc_ce ~ ", collapsed_rhs)), data = national_from_panel)
ic_collapsed <- lm(as.formula(paste0("ic_ce ~ ", collapsed_rhs)), data = national_from_panel)

national_from_panel <- national_from_panel |>
  mutate(
    cc_ce_hat = predict(cc_collapsed),
    ic_ce_hat = predict(ic_collapsed),
    cc_gap = cc_ce - cc_ce_hat,
    ic_gap = ic_ce - ic_ce_hat
  )
Show code 
gap_comparison <- bind_rows(
  national_annual |>
    transmute(date, cc_gap, ic_gap, source = "National (FRED-based)"),
  national_from_panel |>
    transmute(date, cc_gap, ic_gap, source = "Collapsed state panel (CPS, no FE)"),
  annual_gap_summary |>
    transmute(date, cc_gap = cc_ce_gap, ic_gap = ic_ce_gap, source = "State panel (CPS, state FE)")
) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = c(
    "National (FRED-based)",
    "Collapsed state panel (CPS, no FE)",
    "State panel (CPS, state FE)"
  )))

p_cc_compare <- ggplot(gap_comparison, aes(date, cc_gap, color = source)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0073C2", "#E64B35", "grey30")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "CC / CE Gap", subtitle = "Observed minus composition-predicted", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_ic_compare <- ggplot(gap_comparison, aes(date, ic_gap, color = source)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#EFC000", "#E64B35", "grey30")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "IC / CE Gap", subtitle = "Observed minus composition-predicted", x = NULL, y = NULL)

wrap_elements(p_cc_compare + theme(legend.position = "top")) /
  wrap_elements(p_ic_compare + theme(legend.position = "top"))

The three-way comparison reveals both reassuring consistency and informative differences. All three approaches—the national FRED-based model (Section 7.2), the collapsed state panel (CPS-based, no FE), and the state panel with state FE—agree on the broad time path: residuals near zero through the mid-2000s, a recessionary positive spike in 2009, and a persistent negative drift beginning around 2014. This convergence across different data sources and specifications indicates that the post-2014 negative gap is a robust feature of the data, not an artifact of any single modeling choice.

The differences between the approaches are also instructive. The national FRED-based gap and the collapsed CPS-based gap occasionally diverge (e.g., the collapsed panel shows a larger negative gap in 2017 and 2021), reflecting measurement differences between the FRED national aggregates and the CPS state-level composition shares aggregated to the national level. The state-panel model with state FE generally produces a smoother gap series because state fixed effects absorb persistent cross-state level differences that would otherwise inflate residuals. The state-FE gap is therefore the preferred specification for tracking the residual over time: it isolates the portion of claims intensity not accounted for by either composition or time-invariant state characteristics.

For IC/CE, the gaps are proportionally larger than for CC/CE. This is consistent with initial claims being a flow measure at the point of entry into the UI system, where the composition benchmark may have less predictive content relative to short-run administrative and institutional dynamics.

8. Interpretation

The results support a two-part conclusion.

The composition benchmark has substantial reduced-form predictive content. At the national level, by-cause unemployment shares and seasonality account for roughly 90% of the variation in CC/CE and 74% in IC/CE. Relative to completed temporary jobs, higher shares of job leavers and new entrants are associated with significantly lower claims intensity, consistent with these groups’ weaker UI attachment. In the state panel with both state and year fixed effects, the within \(R^2\) drops sharply (roughly 0.09–0.14 for CC/CE, 0.04–0.05 for IC/CE), indicating that much of the raw predictive power of unemployment composition reflects persistent state differences and common national time movement rather than rich within-state identifying variation. This does not invalidate the composition benchmark; it clarifies that the benchmark’s value lies in tracking the aggregate evolution of claims intensity rather than in identifying sharp within-state effects. When year fixed effects are dropped and composition must account for the time path, the within \(R^2\) rises substantially (0.71 for CC/CE, 0.67 for IC/CE), confirming that composition tracks the broad level and cyclical pattern of claims intensity under the historical reduced-form relationship.

But composition does not fully account for the modern shortfall. The gap between observed and benchmark-predicted claims intensity is persistently negative from roughly 2014 onward and widens through 2024–2025. Observed claims intensity falls below the level historically associated with the realized unemployment mix. This residual—the portion not captured by the composition benchmark—appears across the national annual model, the state-panel gap model (state FE only), and the collapsed-national comparison, with broadly consistent time paths across all three approaches. The convergence across specifications and data sources indicates a robust empirical regularity rather than a specification artifact.

The residual is consistent with several non-composition factors the literature has identified:

  • Administrative burden: Parolin, Cross, and O’Brien (2023) document that burdens in UI have increased, disproportionately affecting minority families.
  • Employer deterrence: Lachowska, Sorkin, and Woodbury (2025) show that firm effects on claiming are substantial, with high-appeal firms having lower claim rates.
  • Benefit generosity: Anderson and Meyer (1997) established that the benefit elasticity of UI receipt is approximately 0.5; declining real generosity would reduce claiming.
  • State policy tightening: Vroman (2018) documented that several states shortened maximum benefit durations and increased denial rates after the Great Recession.
  • Racial and demographic disparities: Kuka and Stuart (2025) show persistent gaps in UI receipt by race that operate through claiming conditional on eligibility, not eligibility itself.
  • Information frictions and stigma: Wandner and Stettner (2000) found that perceived ineligibility was the dominant reason for non-application among eligible workers.

This paper does not identify which of these channels dominates. The reduced-form design lacks the individual-level variation in eligibility, employer behavior, or administrative friction needed for that identification. What it does establish is the quantitative benchmark: how much of the variation in claims intensity is accounted for by the observable composition of unemployment under the historical reduced-form relationship, and therefore how large the residual is that mechanism-specific studies must collectively explain.

9. Conclusion

The composition of unemployment accounts for a meaningful share of the variation in UI claims intensity under the historical reduced-form relationship but does not fully account for the modern shortfall. The by-cause composition of unemployment—particularly the shares of job leavers and new entrants relative to the near-neutral completed-temp-job category—tracks the broad level and cyclical pattern of claims intensity at the national level and in state-panel models where within-state and within-year fixed effects absorb the aggregate confounds that a single national time series cannot isolate. The remaining gap is substantial, has turned persistently negative since roughly 2014, and has widened through 2024–2025.

This paper provides a composition-based benchmark for UI claims intensity and shows that recent claims intensity falls below the level historically associated with the realized unemployment mix. The literature has long recognized that job losers are more UI-relevant than new entrants, but it has not systematically estimated how much reduced-form explanatory leverage that compositional fact provides in a panel setting. The answer is: substantial, but not sufficient. The unexplained residual is large and growing, indicating that a complete account of low UI claims intensity requires understanding both the composition of the unemployment pool and the non-composition factors that shape claiming behavior.

The value of the composition benchmark rests on its institutional content, not on fit alone. Reason-for-unemployment categories are not data-mined predictors; they map directly onto the eligibility architecture of the UI system, giving the benchmark a clear interpretation that generic macro covariates would lack. Other variable sets that comove with the same cyclical and secular forces could also track the national time path reasonably well, but they would not answer the question the benchmark is designed to address: how much of the observed path of claims intensity is consistent with shifts in who becomes unemployed and how close those individuals are to the UI system’s historically intended beneficiaries? The composition benchmark is useful not because it is the only variable set that could fit the data, but because it is the one whose fit has direct institutional content.

Three implications follow. First, the by-cause unemployment mix offers a conceptually principled and empirically useful benchmark for UI claims intensity—one grounded in the structure of the program itself. Second, the residual gap between observed and composition-predicted claims intensity quantifies the target that institutional, administrative, and behavioral explanations must collectively account for. Third, the composition channel is likely to become more important as the structure of the labor market continues to evolve, with shifts in occupational mix, gig employment, and immigration patterns all affecting who shows up in the unemployment count and how close they are to the UI system’s originally intended beneficiaries.
